one_liner: LD_PRELOAD user-space persistent-memory file system layered on ext4 DAX; cuts POSIX data-path overhead versus ext4 DAX and NOVA.
what_it_does: SplitFS (SOSP'19) splits a PM file system in two: an LD_PRELOAD library (built on NVSL Quill's glibc-call interception) serves reads, overwrites and appends from memory-mapped files with processor loads and stores, while ext4 DAX in a patched Linux 4.13 kernel handles metadata. Applications run unmodified through the POSIX API (open, pread64, pwrite64, fsync, ftruncate and others listed in the README; the rest pass through to the kernel), and each process picks a POSIX, sync or strict consistency mode. Only files under the hard-coded /mnt/pmem_emul mount, referenced by absolute path, are handled.
how_it_is_fast: Reads and overwrites avoid the syscall and VFS path entirely by copying to and from mmapped DAX file regions. Appends are written with non-temporal stores (MOVNTI=1 in common.mk) into pre-allocated, pre-mapped staging files, and a new relink() syscall later moves those extents into the target file without copying the data. Strict mode adds an operation log in PM for atomicity.
when_to_use: Research or prototyping on Intel Optane DC PMM (or memmap-emulated PM) where append- and overwrite-heavy apps such as LevelDB/YCSB or SQLite/TPC-C dominate
Comparing PM file-system designs: the repo ships scripts for ext4-DAX, NOVA-strict, NOVA-relaxed, PMFS and SplitFS on YCSB, TPC-C, rsync, tar, git, LMDB, Filebench and FIO
Studying the relink/staging-file technique for append atomicity without data copies
Single-process workloads on a bare-metal Ubuntu 16.04/18.04 box you can boot into the bundled 4.13 kernel
when_not_to_use: Anything on ordinary SSDs or NVMe: it needs DAX-capable persistent memory, and Intel has discontinued Optane
Production or modern kernels: it needs the patched Linux 4.13 kernel for relink (issue #46 asks about other kernels), and the last commit was 2021-12-14
Multi-threaded writers: open issues #64 (fio multi-thread and random writes trip an assertion in tbl_mmaps.c) and #75 (multithreaded SQLite TPC-C fails), plus #27 on multi-thread correctness
Crash-consistency-critical deployments: open issues #66 (strict-mode append recovery loses data when inode numbers change) and #67 (rename crash consistency)
Metadata-heavy workloads: the experiments page says SplitFS has a modest overhead on metadata-intensive utilities such as rsync

integration.dependencies: patched Linux 4.13 kernel (relink syscall), ext4 mounted with -o dax on a PM device, Boost, bundled liblfds711, glibc (calls intercepted via Quill)
integration.min_toolchain: gcc with -O3 -m64 (common.mk); Ubuntu 16.04/18.04; compiler version not stated
integration.platforms: x86-64 Intel with clflush or clflushopt, bare metal (no VM), at least 32 GB DRAM and 4 cores per README
integration.thread_safety: Locks are present, but multi-threaded write workloads fail per open issues #64, #75 and #27
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — POSIX API is unchanged via LD_PRELOAD, but only for absolute paths under /mnt/pmem_emul, only for the intercepted calls, and only with the custom kernel

gotchas: The README says the 5.8x microbenchmark appends 128 MB and does an fsync() at the end, but micro/rw_experiment.c has no fsync: it times only the pwrite64 loop with gettimeofday and calls close() after the timer. With LEDGER_YCSB=1 (as the README build step sets) DR_SIZE is 256 MB, so all 128 MB lands in one pre-mapped staging file and the relink that attaches it to the file happens at close, outside the timed region
The workload is pwrite64 at increasing offsets on a file opened without O_TRUNC; the README removes the file between runs, and a stale test.txt turns the appends into overwrites
Build-time workload switches (LEDGER_YCSB, LEDGER_TPCC and others in common.mk) change staging-file sizes and counts, so results depend on which flag the library was compiled with
License mismatch: the LICENSE file is Apache-2.0 but the README says UT Austin holds copyright and asks commercial users to contact the authors; the kernel/ tree is GPL
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick SplitFS when you need unmodified POSIX applications to keep ext4 DAX as the metadata layer and want per-process consistency modes; MadFS (also user-space, up to 3.6x over ext4-DAX on concurrent workloads) is the better choice for multi-threaded writers, WineFS (same lab) for mmap-heavy apps on a kernel PM file system, and Trio/ArckFS reports beating SplitFS on LevelDB.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README run of micro/rw_experiment.c (gcc -O3, 4 KB sequential pwrite64 appends totalling 128 MB): ext4-DAX 0.33M vs SplitFS 1.92M appends/sec (5.8x), with the relink-on-close excluded from timing and no fsync despite the README text; CPU not named for that run. The SOSP'19 paper (peer-reviewed; PDF blocked here, not opened) and the experiments page report 4-12x lower software overhead than NOVA or ext4 DAX and up to 2x on data-intensive applications, on an Intel Xeon E3-1225 v5 with 32 GB DRAM running Ubuntu 16.04 with emulated or Optane PM.
status_note: Abandoned research artifact (last commit 2021-12-14, 171 stars, several open crash and correctness issues); Apache-2.0 LICENSE file but README asks commercial users to contact UT Austin, and it is tied to Linux 4.13 and discontinued Optane hardware.
